section.heading: 2.6. Limits at Infinity; Horizontal Asymptotes
section.paragraph: In Sections 2.2 and 2.4 we investigated infinite limits and vertical asymptotes of a curve $$y = f(x)$$ . There we let $$x$$ approach a number and the result was that the values of $$y$$ became arbitrarily large (positive or negative). In this section we let $$x$$ become arbitrarily large (positive or negative) and see what happens to $$y$$ .
section.heading: Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes
section.paragraph: Let’s begin by investigating the behavior of the function $$f$$ defined by
as $$x$$ becomes large. The table below gives values of this function correct to six decimal places, and the graph of $$f$$ has been drawn by a computer in Figure 1.

image.alt: Details A horizontal line and a curve are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal line labeled y = 1 is drawn from the second quadrant to the first quadrant by crossing the positive y axis. The curve, y = (x^2 minus 1)/(x^2 + 1), is symmetric about the y axis. It enters the second quadrant below the horizontal line, goes down and to the right, veering away from it, concave down, crosses the negative x axis at (negative 1, 0), becoming concave up, and reaches its low point on the negative y axis. It then enters into the fourth quadrant, mirrors its earlier path, goes up and to the right, crosses the positive x axis at (1, 0), then veers toward the horizontal line y = 1, approaches it, and exits the viewing window very closely below y = 1.

section.paragraph: You can see that as $$x$$ grows larger and larger, the values of $$f(x)$$ get closer and closer to $$1$$ . (The graph of $$f$$ approaches the horizontal line $$y = 1$$ as we look to the right.) In fact, it seems that we can make the values of $$f(x)$$ as close as we like to $$1$$ by taking $$x$$ sufficiently large. This situation is expressed symbolically by writing
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{x^{2} - 1}{x^{2} + 1} = 1$$
In general, we use the notation
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = L$$
to indicate that the values of $$f(x)$$ approach $$L$$ as $$x$$ becomes larger and larger.

note.source_type: Intuitive Definition of a Limit at Infinity
note.title: Intuitive Definition of a Limit at Infinity
note.heading: Intuitive Definition of a Limit at Infinity
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ be a function defined on some interval $$(a,\infty)$$ . Then
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = L$$
means that the values of $$f(x)$$ can be made arbitrarily close to $$L$$ by requiring $$x$$ to be sufficiently large.

section.paragraph: Another notation for $$\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = L$$ is
$$\left. f(x)\rightarrow L {as} \right.\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$
The symbol $$\infty$$ does not represent a number. Nonetheless, the expression $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = L$$ is often read as

list.item: “the limit of $$f(x)$$ , as $$x$$ approaches infinity, is $$L$$ ”

section.paragraph: or

list.item: “the limit of $$f(x)$$ , as $$x$$ becomes infinite, is $$L$$ ”

section.paragraph: or

list.item: “the limit of $$f(x)$$ , as $$x$$ increases without bound, is $$L$$ ”

section.paragraph: The meaning of such phrases is given by Definition 1. A more precise definition, similar to the $$\varepsilon$$ , $$\delta$$ definition of Section 2.4, is given at the end of this section.

Geometric illustrations of Definition 1 are shown in Figure 2. Notice that there are many ways for the graph of $$f$$ to approach the line $$y = L$$ (which is called a horizontal asymptote) as we look to the far right of each graph.

image.alt: Details Three graphs display a line and a curve on the x y coordinate plane. In the first graph, a horizontal line y = L is drawn from the second quadrant to the first quadrant far away from the x axis. The curve labeled y = f(x) enters the second quadrant above the horizontal line, goes up and to the right, reaches its high point, then goes down, crosses the positive y axis, concaves up, and reaches its low point in the first quadrant above the x axis. It then goes up and to the right, now concave down, veers toward the horizontal line while approaching it, and exits very closely below the horizontal line y = L. In the second graph, a horizontal line y = L is drawn from the second quadrant to the first quadrant, a little away from the origin. The curve labeled y = f(x) enters the second quadrant, goes down and to the right, concave up, crosses the positive y axis, enters into the first quadrant, veers toward the horizontal line y = L while approaching it, and exits the viewing window very closely above the line in the first quadrant. In the third graph, a horizontal line y = L is drawn from the second quadrant to the first quadrant. The curve labeled y = f(x) enters the second quadrant below y = L, goes up and to the right, intersects y = L, reaches its high point in the first quadrant, goes down and to the right to reach a low point, again rises to a high point and falls to a low point. The same wave pattern then repeats thereafter. As the curve proceeds rightward, the high and low points of the curve approach the horizontal line, that is, the amplitude gets progressively lower.

section.paragraph: Referring back to Figure 1, we see that for numerically large negative values of $$x$$ , the values of $$f(x)$$ are close to $$1$$ . By letting $$x$$ decrease through negative values without bound, we can make $$f(x)$$ as close to $$1$$ as we like. This is expressed by writing
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{x^{2} - 1}{x^{2} + 1} = 1$$
The general definition is as follows.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ be a function defined on some interval $$( - \infty,a)$$ . Then
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x) = L$$
means that the values of $$f(x)$$ can be made arbitrarily close to $$L$$ by requiring $$x$$ to be sufficiently large negative.

section.paragraph: Again, the symbol $$- \infty$$ does not represent a number, but the expression $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x) = L$$ is often read as

list.item: “the limit of $$f(x)$$ , as $$x$$ approaches negative infinity, is $$L$$ ”

section.paragraph: Definition 2 is illustrated in Figure 3. Notice that the graph approaches the line $$y = L$$ as we look to the far left of each graph.

image.alt: Details Two graphs display a line and a curve on the x y coordinate plane. In the first graph, a horizontal line labeled y = L is drawn from the second quadrant to the first quadrant. The curve labeled y = f(x) enters the second quadrant very closely above the line y = L, goes up and to the right, veering away from it, now concave down, reaches its high point in the second quadrant, goes down and to the right into the first quadrant, now concave up, reaches its low point, and again goes up and to the right. In the second graph, a horizontal line y = L is drawn from the second quadrant to the first quadrant. The curve labeled y = f(x) enters the second quadrant from the left, below the line y = L, goes down and to the right, veering away from it, now concave up, reaches its low point in the second quadrant, goes up and to the right by intersecting the line y = L, now concave down, reaches a high point in the second quadrant, then goes down and to the right into the first quadrant, again intersects the horizontal line y = L.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The line $$y = L$$ is called a horizontal asymptote of the curve $$y = f(x)$$ if either
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = L$$
or
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x) = L$$

section.paragraph: For instance, the curve illustrated in Figure 1 has the line $$y = 1$$ as a horizontal asymptote because
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{x^{2} - 1}{x^{2} + 1} = 1$$
An example of a curve with two horizontal asymptotes is $$y = \tan^{- 1}x$$ . (See Figure 4.) In fact,
$${\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\tan^{- 1}x = - \frac{\pi}{2}} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\tan^{- 1}x = \frac{\pi}{2}}$$

so both of the lines $$y = - \pi \slash 2$$ and $$y = \pi \slash 2$$ are horizontal asymptotes. (This follows from the fact that the lines $$x = \pm \pi \slash 2$$ are vertical asymptotes of the graph of the tangent function.)

A horizontal line is drawn from the second quadrant to the first quadrant, crossing the y axis at (0, pi/2). Another horizontal line is drawn from the third quadrant to the fourth quadrant, crossing the y axis at (0, negative pi/2). The curve enters the third quadrant above the horizontal line y = negative pi/2, veering away from it as the curve goes up and to the right through the origin, then enters into the first quadrant, veers toward the horizontal line y = pi/2, approaches it as the curve proceeds to the right, and exits the viewing window very closely below the horizontal line y = pi/2.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Find the infinite limits, limits at infinity, and asymptotes for the function $$f$$ whose graph is shown in Figure 5.

image.alt: Details A function with three parts is graphed on the x y coordinate plane on the grid lines. The x axis is displayed from negative 4 to 8 in increments of 1 unit. The y axis is displayed from negative 4 to 6 in increments of 1 unit. The first part enters the second quadrant from the left, very closely above y = 2, goes up and to the right, concave up, and exits the second quadrant to the left of x = negative 1 at the top. The second part enters the second quadrant at the top, very close to the right of x = negative 1, goes down and to the right, concave up, crosses the positive y axis at approximately (0, 0.2), crosses the positive x axis at approximately (0.02, 0), enters into the fourth quadrant, goes down and to the right, now concave down, and exits the fourth quadrant very closely to the left of x = 2. The third part enters the first quadrant very closely to the right of x = 2, goes down and to the right, concave up, reaches a low point at approximately (3.2, 1.2), goes up and to the right, now concave down, veering toward y = 4 while approaching it, and exits very closely below y = 4.

example.paragraph: Solution We see that the values of $$f(x)$$ become large as $$\left. x\rightarrow - 1 \right.$$ from both sides, so
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 1}f(x) = \infty$$
Notice that $$f(x)$$ becomes large negative as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ from the left, but large positive as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ from the right. So
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}f(x) = - \infty$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2^{+}}f(x) = \infty$$
Thus both of the lines $$x = - 1$$ and $$x = 2$$ are vertical asymptotes.
As $$x$$ becomes large, it appears that $$f(x)$$ approaches $$4$$ . But as $$x$$ decreases through negative values, $$f(x)$$ approaches $$2$$ . So
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = 4$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x) = 2$$
This means that both $$y = 4$$ and $$y = 2$$ are horizontal asymptotes.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x}$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{x}$$ .
Solution Observe that when $$x$$ is large, $$1 \slash x$$ is small. For instance,
In fact, by taking $$x$$ large enough, we can make $$1 \slash x$$ as close to $$0$$ as we please. Therefore, according to Definition 1, we have
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x} = 0$$
Similar reasoning shows that when $$x$$ is large negative, $$1 \slash x$$ is small negative, so we also have
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{x} = 0$$
It follows that the line $$y = 0$$ (the $$x$$ -axis) is a horizontal asymptote of the curve $$y = 1 \slash x$$ . (This is a hyperbola; see Figure 6.)

image.alt: Details A horizontal line and a curve are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal line is drawn on the x axis. The curve labeled y = 1/x has two parts. The first part lies entirely in the third quadrant. It enters the third quadrant very close to the x axis, veering away from it as the curve gradually goes down and to the right, concave down, veering toward the y axis as the curve approaches it. The second part of the curve lies entirely in the first quadrant. It enters the first quadrant at the top, very close to the y axis, falls steeply to the right, concaves up, veering toward the x axis, running almost parallel to the x axis very close to it.

section.heading: Evaluating Limits at Infinity
section.paragraph: Most of the Limit Laws that were given in Section 2.3 also hold for limits at infinity. It can be proved that the Limit Laws listed in Section 2.3 (with the exception of Laws 10 and 11 ) are also valid if “ $$\left. x\rightarrow a \right.$$ ” is replaced by “ $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ ” or “ $$\left. x\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ .” In particular, if we combine Laws 6 and 7 with the results of Example 2, we obtain the following important rule for calculating limits.

note.title: Theorem
note.heading: Theorem
note.paragraph: If $$r > 0$$ is a rational number, then
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x^{r}} = 0$$
If $$r > 0$$ is a rational number such that $$x^{r}$$ is defined for all $$x$$ , then
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{x^{r}} = 0$$

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Evaluate the following limit and indicate which properties of limits are used at each stage.
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1}$$
Solution As $$x$$ becomes large, both numerator and denominator become large, so it isn’t obvious what happens to their ratio. We need to do some preliminary algebra.

To evaluate the limit at infinity of any rational function, we first divide both the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $$x$$ that occurs in the denominator. (We may assume that $$x \neq 0$$ , since we are interested only in large values of $$x$$ .) In this case the highest power of $$x$$ in the denominator is $$x^{2}$$ , so we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{x^{2}}}{\frac{5x^{2} + 4x + 1}{x^{2}}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3 - \frac{1}{x} - \frac{2}{x^{2}}}{5 + \frac{4}{x} + \frac{1}{x^{2}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1}} = {\frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( {3 - \frac{1}{x} - \frac{2}{x^{2}}} \right)}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( {5 + \frac{4}{x} + \frac{1}{x^{2}}} \right)} \left( {{by Limit Law}5} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1}} = {\frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}3 - \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x} - 2\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}}}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}5 + 4\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x} + \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}}} \left( {{by}1,2,{and}3} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1}} = {\frac{3 - 0 - 0}{5 + 0 + 0} \left( {{by}8{and Theorem}5} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1}} = \frac{3}{5}} \end{array}$$

A similar calculation shows that the limit as $$\left. x\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ is also $$\frac{3}{5}$$ . Figure 7 illustrates the results of these calculations by showing how the graph of the given rational function approaches the horizontal asymptote $$y = \frac{3}{5} = 0.6$$ .

image.alt: Details A horizontal line and a curve are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal line labeled y = 0.6 is drawn from the second quadrant to the first quadrant. The curve enters the second quadrant from the left above the horizontal line y = 0.6, goes up and to the right as it veers away from it, reaches its high point in the second quadrant, goes down and to the right by intersecting the line y = 0.6, then crosses the negative x axis, concave up, and reaches its low point in the third quadrant near the y axis. It then rises steeply to the right, concave down, crosses the negative y axis, then crosses the positive x axis at (1, 0), approaches the line y = 0.6, and exits the first quadrant very closely below it.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find the horizontal asymptotes of the graph of the function
Solution Dividing both numerator and denominator by $$x$$ (which is the highest power of $$x$$ in the denominator) and using the properties of limits, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\sqrt{2x^{2} + 1}}{3x - 5}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\frac{\sqrt{2x^{2} + 1}}{x}}{\frac{3x - 5}{x}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\sqrt{\frac{2x^{2} + 1}{x^{2}}}}{\frac{3x - 5}{x}} {({since}\sqrt{x^{2}} = x{for}x > 0)}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\sqrt{2x^{2} + 1}}{3x - 5}} = {\frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt{2 + \frac{1}{x^{2}}}}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( {3 - \frac{5}{x}} \right)} = \frac{\sqrt{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}2 + \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}}}}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}3 - 5\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x}} = \frac{\sqrt{2 + 0}}{3 - 5 \cdot 0} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}}} \end{array}$$
Therefore the line $$y = \sqrt{2} \slash 3$$ is a horizontal asymptote of the graph of $$f$$ .

In computing the limit as $$\left. x\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ , we must remember that for $$x < 0$$ , we have $$\sqrt{x^{2}} = |x| = - x$$ . So when we divide the numerator by $$x$$ , for $$x < 0$$ we get
Therefore

$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{\sqrt{2x^{2} + 1}}{3x - 5} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{- \sqrt{2 + \frac{1}{x^{2}}}}{3 - \frac{5}{x}} = \frac{- \sqrt{2 + \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}}}}{3 - 5\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{x}} = - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}$$
Thus the line $$y = - \sqrt{2} \slash 3$$ is also a horizontal asymptote. See Figure 8.

Another horizontal line y = sqrt(2)/3 is drawn from the second quadrant to the first quadrant. The function has two parts. The first part enters the third quadrant from the left above the horizontal line y = negative sqrt(2)/3, goes up and to the right as it veers away from it, reaches its high point on the negative y axis, then falls steeply to the right in the fourth quadrant by crossing the horizontal line y = negative sqrt(2)/3, and exits to the right of the y axis at the bottom. The second part enters the first quadrant at the top, a little away from the y axis, goes down and to the right, concave up, veering toward the x axis, and exits above it.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Compute $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}{({\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} - x})}$$ .

Solution Because both $$\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}$$ and $$x$$ are large when $$x$$ is large, it’s difficult to see what happens to their difference, so we use algebra to rewrite the function. We first multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate radical:

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}{({\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} - x})}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}{({\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} - x})} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} + x}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} + x}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}{({\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} - x})}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{(x^{2} + 1) - x^{2}}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} + x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} + x}}} \end{array}$$
We can think of the given function as having a denominator of $$1$$ .
Notice that the denominator of this last expression $$(\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} + x)$$ becomes large as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ (it’s bigger than $$x$$ ). So
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}(\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} - x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} + x} = 0$$
Figure 9 illustrates this result.

image.alt: Details A horizontal line and a curve are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal line is drawn on the x axis. The curve labeled y = sqrt(x^2 + 1) minus x, enters the second quadrant at the top left of the viewing window, goes down and to the right, concave up, crosses the y axis at (0, 1), enters into the first quadrant, and continues to extend toward the x axis, almost coincides with the x axis before exiting near the right extreme of the x axis.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2^{+}}\arctan\left( \frac{1}{x - 2} \right)$$ .

Solution If we let $$t = 1 \slash \left( {x - 2} \right)$$ , we know that $$\left. t\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 2^{+} \right.$$ . Therefore, by the second equation in (4), we have
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2^{+}}\arctan\left( \frac{1}{x - 2} \right) = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}\arctan t = \frac{\pi}{2}$$

section.paragraph: The graph of the natural exponential function $$y = e^{ x}$$ has the line $$y = 0$$ (the $$x$$ -axis) as a horizontal asymptote. (The same is true of any exponential function with base $$b > 1$$ .) In fact, from the graph in Figure 10 and the corresponding table of values, we see that
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}e^{ x} = 0$$
Notice that the values of $$e^{ x}$$ approach $$0$$ very rapidly.

The y axis is displayed from below 0 to beyond 1 in increments of 1 unit. The curve labeled y = e^x, enters the second quadrant, initially almost coinciding with the negative x axis, begins to veer away from it while rising, concave up, crosses the y axis at (0, 1), and continues to go upward to the right into the first quadrant.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}e^{1 \slash x}$$ .

The problem-solving strategy for Examples 6 and 7 is introducing something extra (see Principles of Problem Solving following Chapter 1). Here, the something extra, the auxiliary aid, is the new variable $$t$$ .
Solution If we let $$t = 1 \slash x$$ , we know that $$\left. t\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{-} \right.$$ . Therefore, by (6),
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}e^{1 \slash x} = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow - \infty}e^{ t} = 0$$
(See Exercise 81.)

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\sin x$$ .

Solution As $$x$$ increases, the values of $$\sin x$$ oscillate between $$1$$ and $$- 1$$ infinitely often and so they don’t approach any definite number. Thus $$\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}\sin x$$ does not exist.

section.heading: Infinite Limits at Infinity
section.paragraph: The notation
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = \infty$$
is used to indicate that the values of $$f(x)$$ become large as $$x$$ becomes large. Similar meanings are attached to the following symbols:
$${\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x) = \infty} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = - \infty} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x) = - \infty}$$

example.heading: Example 9
example.paragraph: Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x^{3}$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}x^{3}$$ .
Solution When $$x$$ becomes large, $$x^{3}$$ also becomes large. For instance,
In fact, we can make $$x^{3}$$ as big as we like by requiring $$x$$ to be large enough. Therefore we can write
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x^{3} = \infty$$
Similarly, when $$x$$ is large negative, so is $$x^{3}$$ . Thus
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}x^{3} = - \infty$$
These limit statements can also be seen from the graph of $$y = x^{3}$$ in Figure 11.

The curve labeled y = x^3 enters the third quadrant at the bottom left, goes up and to the right, concave down, briefly levels out at the origin (0, 0), goes up and to the right in the first quadrant, now concave up, and exits the top right of the viewing window.

$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}e^{ x} = \infty$$
but, as Figure 12 demonstrates, $$y = e^{ x}$$ becomes large as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ at a much faster rate than $$y = x^{3}$$ .

example.heading: Example 10
example.paragraph: Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( {x^{2} - x} \right)$$ .
Solution Limit Law 2 says that the limit of a difference is the difference of the limits, provided that these limits exist. We cannot use Law 2 here because
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x^{2} = \infty$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x = \infty$$
In general, the Limit Laws can’t be applied to infinite limits because $$\infty$$ is not a number ( $$\infty - \infty$$ can’t be defined). However, we can write
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}(x^{2} - x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x(x - 1) = \infty$$
because both $$x$$ and $$x - 1$$ become arbitrarily large and so their product does too.

example.heading: Example 11
example.paragraph: Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{x^{2} + x}{3 - x}$$ .
Solution As in Example 3, we divide the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $$x$$ in the denominator, which is simply $$x$$ :
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{x^{2} + x}{3 - x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{x + 1}{\frac{3}{x} - 1} = - \infty$$
because $$\left. x + 1\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ and $$\left. 3 \slash x - 1\rightarrow 0 - 1 = - 1 \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ .

section.paragraph: The next example shows that by using infinite limits at infinity, together with intercepts, we can get a rough idea of the graph of a polynomial without having to plot a large number of points.

example.heading: Example 12
example.paragraph: Sketch the graph of $$y = \left( {x - 2} \right)^{4}\left( {x + 1} \right)^{3}\left( {x - 1} \right)$$ by finding its intercepts and its limits as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ and as $$\left. x\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ .

Solution The $$y$$ -intercept is $$f(0) = ( - 2)^{4}(1)^{3}( - 1) = - 16$$ and the $$x$$ -intercepts are found by setting $$y = 0$$ : $$x = 2, - 1,1$$ . Notice that since $$\left( {x - 2} \right)^{4}$$ is never negative, the function doesn’t change sign at $$2$$ ; thus the graph doesn’t cross the $$x$$ -axis at $$2$$ . The graph crosses the axis at $$- 1$$ and $$1$$ .
When $$x$$ is large positive, all three factors are large, so
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( {x - 2} \right)^{4}\left( {x + 1} \right)^{3}\left( {x - 1} \right) = \infty$$
When $$x$$ is large negative, the first factor is large positive and the second and third factors are both large negative, so
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\left( {x - 2} \right)^{4}\left( {x + 1} \right)^{3}\left( {x - 1} \right) = \infty$$
Combining this information, we give a rough sketch of the graph in Figure 13.

section.heading: Precise Definitions
section.paragraph: Definition 1 can be stated precisely as follows.

note.source_type: Precise Definition of a Limit at Infinity
note.title: Precise Definition of a Limit at Infinity
note.heading: Precise Definition of a Limit at Infinity
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ be a function defined on some interval $$(a,\infty)$$ . Then
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = L$$
means that for every $$\varepsilon > 0$$ there is a corresponding number $$N$$ such that
$${{if} x > N} {then} {\left| {f(x) - L} \right| < \varepsilon}$$

section.paragraph: In words, this says that the values of $$f(x)$$ can be made arbitrarily close to $$L$$ (within a distance $$\varepsilon$$ , where $$\varepsilon$$ is any positive number) by requiring $$x$$ to be sufficiently large (larger than $$N$$ , where $$N$$ depends on $$\varepsilon$$ ). Graphically, it says that by keeping $$x$$ large enough (larger than some number $$N$$ ) we can make the graph of $$f$$ lie between the given horizontal lines $$y = L - \varepsilon$$ and $$y = L + \varepsilon$$ as in Figure 14. This must be true no matter how small we choose $$\varepsilon$$ .

example.heading: Example 14
example.paragraph: Use Definition 7 to prove that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x} = 0$$ .
Solution Given $$\varepsilon > 0$$ , we want to find $$N$$ such that
$${{if} x > N} {then} {\left| {\frac{1}{x} - 0} \right| < \varepsilon}$$
In computing the limit we may assume that $$x > 0$$ . Then $$\left. 1 \slash x < \varepsilon\Leftrightarrow x > 1 \slash \varepsilon \right.$$ . Let’s choose $$N = 1 \slash \varepsilon$$ . So
$${{if} x > N = \frac{1}{\varepsilon}} {then} {\left| {\frac{1}{x} - 0} \right| = \frac{1}{x} < \varepsilon}$$
Therefore, by Definition 7,
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x} = 0$$
Figure 18 illustrates the proof by showing some values of $$\varepsilon$$ and the corresponding values of $$N$$ .

note.title: Precise Definition of an Infinite Limit at Infinity
note.heading: Precise Definition of an Infinite Limit at Infinity
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ be a function defined on some interval $$(a,\infty)$$ . Then
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = \infty$$
means that for every positive number $$M$$ there is a corresponding positive number $$N$$ such that
$${{if} x > N} {then} {f(x) > M}$$

section.paragraph: Similar definitions apply when the symbol $$\infty$$ is replaced by $$- \infty$$ . (See Exercise 80.)
